## The 4 Preliminary Preparations (Pubbakaraṇa)
Sweeping the place, lighting the lamps, setting out drinking and washing water, and spreading the seats—these four are called the "Preliminary Preparations" (Pubbakaraṇa) of the Uposatha.

## The 5 Preliminary Duties (Pubbakicca)
Conveying consent, conveying purity, announcing the season, counting the monks, and conveying the instruction—these five are called the "Preliminary Duties" (Pubbakicca) of the Uposatha.

## The 4 Factors of Timeliness (Pattakalla)
It being the Uposatha day, the presence of as many monks as are required for the act, the absence of common offenses (sabhāgāpatti), and the absence of excluded persons in the assembly—this is called "Timeliness" (Pattakalla).

Having completed the preliminary preparations and preliminary duties, with the consent of the harmonious Saṅgha of monks who have declared their offenses, I shall perform the recitation of the Pātimokkha for the satisfaction of the Saṅgha.

## Recitation of the Introduction (Nidānuddesa)
Venerable Sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. Today is the fifteenth day Uposatha. If it is the right time for the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha perform the Uposatha and recite the Pātimokkha.

What is the preliminary duty of the Saṅgha? Venerables, report your purity; I shall recite the Pātimokkha. Let all of us who are here listen well and pay close attention. Whoever has an offense should reveal it. If there is no offense, one should remain silent. By your silence, I shall know that the Venerables are pure.

Just as there is a response for one who is questioned individually, so it is proclaimed up to the third time in an assembly such as this. If a monk, while it is being proclaimed up to the third time, remembers an offense and does not reveal it, he is guilty of a deliberate lie (sampajāna-musāvāda). Venerables, a deliberate lie has been called an obstructive state by the Blessed One. Therefore, a monk who remembers an offense and desires purity should reveal the offense he has committed. For by revealing it, there is comfort for him.

Venerables, the Introduction has been recited. In this regard, I ask the Venerables: Are you pure in this? A second time I ask: Are you pure in this? A third time I ask: Are you pure in this? The Venerables are pure in this, therefore they are silent. Thus do I understand it.

## The Introduction is finished.

## Recitation of the Chapter on Defeat (Pārājika)

## In this Pātimokkha, these four rules of Defeat (Pārājika) come for recitation.

## The Training Rule on Sexual Intercourse (Methunadhamma)

Whatever monk, having undertaken the monks' training and system of life, without renouncing the training and without declaring his weakness, should engage in sexual intercourse, even with a female animal, he is defeated and no longer in communion.

## The Training Rule on Taking What is Not Given (Adinnādāna)

Whatever monk should take from a village or from a forest what is not given, in the manner of theft—such that for taking what is not given, kings would seize the thief and kill, imprison, or banish him, saying, "You are a thief, you are a fool, you are a deluded person, you are a robber"—the monk who takes what is not given in such a manner is also defeated and no longer in communion.

## The Training Rule on Human Beings (Manussaviggaha)

Whatever monk should intentionally deprive a human being of life, or should look for a weapon for that purpose, or should praise the beauty of death, or should incite someone to death, saying, "My good man, what is the use of this miserable, wretched life to you? Death is better for you than life"—having such a thought and such an intention...
4:
having such an intention, should in various ways praise the beauty of death or incite someone to death, he too is defeated and no longer in communion.

## The Training Rule on Superior Human States (Uttari-manussadhamma)

Whatever monk, without direct knowledge, should claim for himself a superior human state, a truly noble knowledge and vision capable of destroying defilements, saying, "Thus I know, thus I see," and then at a later time, whether questioned or not questioned, having fallen into an offense and desiring purity, should say, "Friends, not knowing, I said 'I know'; not seeing, I said 'I see'; I spoke empty, false words"—except for overestimation (adhimāna)—he too is defeated and no longer in communion.

Venerables, the four rules of Defeat have been recited. A monk who has fallen into any one of these rules of Defeat no longer obtains communion with the monks as before; he is defeated and no longer in communion. In this regard, I ask the Venerables: Are you pure in these? A second time I ask: Are you pure in these? A third time I ask: Are you pure in these? The Venerables are pure in these, therefore they are silent. Thus do I understand it.

## The Chapter on Defeat is finished.

## Sañcaritta Training Rule

Whatever monk should engage in matchmaking—of a woman to a man or a man to a woman, whether as a wife or a mistress, or even for a temporary encounter—it is a Saṅghādisesa offense.

## Kuṭikāra Training Rule

A monk building a hut for himself by his own begging, where there is no owner, should have it built according to measurement. Herein, this is the measurement: twelve spans by the Sugata's span in length, and seven spans across the interior. Monks should be brought to designate the site. Those monks should designate a site that is without danger and has an open space around it. If the monk should build a hut by his own begging on a site that has danger or lacks an open space, or if he should not bring monks to designate the site, or if he should exceed the measurement, it is a Saṅghādisesa offense.

## Vihārakāra Training Rule

A monk building a large dwelling for himself, where there is an owner, should bring monks to designate the site. Those monks should designate a site that is without danger and has an open space around it. If the monk should build a large dwelling on a site that has danger or lacks an open space, or if he should not bring monks to designate the site, it is a Saṅghādisesa offense.

## Duṭṭhadosa Training Rule

Whatever monk, being angry and malicious, out of dissatisfaction, should accuse another monk of a groundless Pārājika offense, thinking, "Perhaps I can cause him to fall from this holy life"; and if later, whether he is questioned or not, that case is found to be groundless and the monk confesses his malice, it is a Saṅghādisesa offense.

## Aññabhāgiya Training Rule

Whatever monk, being angry and malicious, out of dissatisfaction, taking some point of a different kind of case as a mere pretext, should accuse another monk of a Pārājika offense, thinking, "Perhaps I can cause him to fall from this holy life"; and if later, whether he is questioned or not, that case is found to be of a different kind and the pretext was merely used, and the monk confesses his malice, it is a Saṅghādisesa offense.

## Saṅghabheda Training Rule

Whatever monk should strive for a schism of a harmonious Saṅgha, or should persist in taking up and advocating a case conducive to a schism, that monk should be spoken to by the monks thus: "Venerable sir, do not strive for a schism of a harmonious Saṅgha, or persist in taking up and advocating a case conducive to a schism. Let the venerable one be at peace with the Saṅgha. For a harmonious Saṅgha, being in agreement and without dispute, lives in comfort under a single recitation of the Pātimokkha."

If that monk, being thus spoken to by the monks, should still persist as before, the monks [should admonish] that monk regarding that view...

## Second Aniyata Training Rule

If the seat is not screened and not suitable [for sexual intercourse], but it is suitable for addressing a woman with lewd words, and should any monk sit together with a woman, one-on-one, in such a secluded place; and a trustworthy laywoman, having seen him, should charge him with one of two offenses—either a Saṅghādisesa or a Pācittiya—then the monk, if he admits to the sitting, should be dealt with according to one of the two offenses: a Saṅghādisesa or a Pācittiya; or according to whatever [offense] that trustworthy laywoman may say, so should that monk be dealt with. This offense is also Indefinite (Aniyata).

## Training Rule on Old Robes

Should any monk have an old robe washed, dyed, or beaten by a nun who is not a relative, there is an offense of forfeiture and confession.

## Training Rule on Receiving Robes

Should any monk receive a robe from the hand of a nun who is not a relative, except in exchange, there is an offense of forfeiture and confession.

## Training Rule on Requesting from an Unrelated Person

Should any monk request a robe from a male householder or a female householder who is not a relative, except at the proper time, there is an offense of forfeiture and confession. In this case, the proper time is when the monk's robe has been stolen or destroyed; this is the proper time in this case.

## Training Rule Beyond That [Limit]

If a male householder or a female householder who is not a relative should offer many robes to that monk, inviting him to take as many as he likes, that monk may accept robes from them at most to the extent of an inner and an upper robe. If he should accept more than that, there is an offense of forfeiture and confession.

## First Training Rule on the Prepared [Robe Fund]

If a robe fund has been set aside by a male householder or a female householder who is not a relative, specifically for a certain monk, with the thought: "Having bought a robe with this robe fund, I will provide a robe for the monk named so-and-so," and if that monk, [approaching] that donor...

If a monk, not being invited beforehand, approaches [the donor] and makes a special arrangement regarding a robe, saying: "Friend, please exchange this robe-fund for such and such a robe and donate it to me," out of a desire for a good robe, it is an offence of Expiation involving Forfeiture (Nissaggiya Pācittiya).

## Dutiya-upakkhaṭa Sikkhāpada
## Dutiya-upakkhaṭa Sikkhāpada

If two householders or two housewives, who are not relatives, have set aside separate robe-funds for a particular monk, saying: "We will exchange these separate robe-funds for separate robes and donate them to such and such a monk," and if that monk, not being invited beforehand, approaches them and makes a special arrangement regarding the robes, saying: "Friends, please exchange these separate robe-funds for such and such a robe and, being two people, donate just one [robe] together," out of a desire for a good robe, it is an offence of Expiation involving Forfeiture.

## Rāja Sikkhāpada

If a king, or a royal official, or a brahmin, or a householder sends a robe-fund by a messenger for a particular monk, saying: "Exchange this robe-fund for a robe and donate it to such and such a monk," and if that messenger approaches that monk and says: "Venerable sir, this robe-fund is brought for you..."
16:
"Please accept this robe-fund that has been brought," that monk should say to that messenger: "Friend, we do not accept robe-funds; we only accept robes that are allowable at the proper time." If that messenger asks that monk: "Venerable sir, is there anyone who is your steward (veyyāvaccakara)?" then, monks, the monk who needs a robe should point out a monastery attendant (ārāmika) or a lay follower (upāsaka), saying: "Friend, this person is the steward of the monks."

If that messenger, having informed the steward, approaches that monk and says: "Venerable sir, I have informed the steward you pointed out; please approach him at the proper time, and he will donate a robe to you." Monks, the monk who needs a robe, having approached the steward, should ask and remind him two or three times, saying: "Friend, I need a robe." If, after asking and reminding him two or three times, he obtains the robe, that is good. If he does not obtain it, he should stand in silence for the purpose of the robe at most four, five, or six times. If, while standing in silence for the purpose of the robe up to six times, he obtains the robe, that is good. If he makes further effort and obtains the robe, it is an offence of Expiation involving Forfeiture. If he does not obtain it, he should either go himself or send a messenger to the place from where the robe-fund was brought for him, saying: "Friends, the robe-fund you sent for a particular monk has not benefited that monk at all..."

## Kosiya Vagga

## Kosiya Sikkhāpada

If a monk has a rug (santhata) made mixed with silk, it is an offence of Expiation involving Forfeiture.

## Suddhakaဠaka Sikkhāpada

If a monk has a rug made of pure black sheep's wool, it is an offence of Expiation involving Forfeiture.

## Dvebhāga Sikkhāpada

When a monk is having a new rug made, two parts of pure black sheep's wool should be taken, a third part of white wool, and a fourth part of brownish-grey (mottled) wool. If a monk has a new rug made without taking two parts of pure black sheep's wool, a third part of white wool, and a fourth part of brownish-grey wool, it is an offence of Expiation involving Forfeiture.

## Chabbassa Sikkhāpada

When a monk has had a new rug made, it should be kept for six years. If, within six years, whether he has abandoned that rug or not, he has another new rug made without the permission of the monks, it is an offence of Expiation involving Forfeiture.

## Nisīdanasanthata Sikkhāpada

When a monk is having a sitting rug (nisīdana-santhata) made, a piece the size of a Sugata-span (Sugatavidatthi) should be taken from all around an old rug in order to disfigure it (or to incorporate parts of the old one). If a monk has a new sitting rug made without taking a piece the size of a Sugata-span from the old rug, it is an offence of Expiation involving Forfeiture.

## Eḷakaloma Sikkhāpada

If sheep's wool should accrue to a monk traveling on a long journey, he may accept it if he so desires. Having accepted it, if there is no one to carry it, he may carry it himself for a distance of at most three yojanas. If he carries it further than three yojanas, even if there is no one to carry it, it is an offence of Expiation involving Forfeiture.

## Eḷakalomadhovāpana Sikkhāpada

If a monk has sheep's wool washed, dyed, or carded by a nun who is not a relative, it is an offence of Expiation involving Forfeiture.

## Rūpiya Sikkhāpada

If a monk accepts gold or silver himself, or has it accepted [by another], or consents to gold or silver being deposited for him, it is an offence of Expiation involving Forfeiture.

## Rūpiyasaṃvohāra Sikkhāpada

If a monk engages in various kinds of exchange (trading) with gold or silver, it is an offence of Expiation involving Forfeiture.

## Kayavikkaya Sikkhāpada
Should any bhikkhu engage in various types of trading (buying and selling), it is an offense of confession involving forfeiture.

## Patta Vagga

## Patta Sikkhāpada
An extra bowl may be kept for at most ten days. For one who lets that period exceed ten days, it is an offense of confession involving forfeiture.

## Ūnapañcabandhana Sikkhāpada
Should any bhikkhu ask for another new bowl when his current bowl has fewer than five mends, it is an offense of confession involving forfeiture. That bowl must be forfeited by that bhikkhu to the assembly of bhikkhus. Whichever bowl is the last (the least desirable) of that assembly of bhikkhus should be given to that bhikkhu with the words: "Bhikkhu, this is your bowl; it is to be kept until it breaks." This is the proper procedure in that case.

## Bhesajja Sikkhāpada
There are these medicines which may be used by sick bhikkhus, namely: ghee, fresh butter, oil, honey, and molasses. Having accepted them, they may be stored and used for at most seven days. For one who lets that period exceed seven days, it is an offense of confession involving forfeiture.

## Bhūtagāma Vagga

## Bhūtagāma Sikkhāpada
For the destruction of vegetation, there is an offense of Pācittiya.

## Aññavādaka Sikkhāpada
For speaking evasively and for harassing the Saṅgha, there is an offense of Pācittiya.

## Ujjhāpanaka Sikkhāpada
For complaining in order to cause others to look down [upon a monk], and for disparaging by pointing out faults, there is an offense of Pācittiya.

Whichever monk, having spread or having caused to be spread in the open a couch, a chair, a mattress, or a stool belonging to the Saṅgha, should depart without putting it away or causing it to be put away, or without asking permission, there is an offense of Pācittiya.

## Dutiya Senāsana Sikkhāpada
Whichever monk, having spread or having caused to be spread bedding in a dwelling belonging to the Saṅgha, should depart without putting it away or causing it to be put away, or without asking permission, there is an offense of Pācittiya.

## Anupakhajja Sikkhāpada
Whichever monk, in a dwelling belonging to the Saṅgha, knowing that another monk has arrived first, should lie down crowding him, thinking, "Whoever finds it cramped will depart," making only this reason of crowding and no other, there is an offense of Pācittiya.

## Nikkaḍḍhana Sikkhāpada
Whichever monk, being angry and displeased, should expel or cause to be expelled another monk from a dwelling belonging to the Saṅgha, there is an offense of Pācittiya.

## Vehāsakuṭi Sikkhāpada
Whichever monk, in a dwelling belonging to the Saṅgha, should sit or lie down on a couch or a chair with removable legs on an upper floor, there is an offense of Pācittiya.

When a monk is having a large dwelling built, he may supervise the fixing of the door-leaf and the door-frame, and the preparation of the window and the door-leaf (including the application of plaster), and the two or three layers of roofing, while standing in a place where there are no green crops. ## Ovāda Sikkhāpada
Whichever monk, without being authorized [by the Saṅgha], should exhort the nuns, there is an offense of Pācittiya.

## Atthaṅgata Sikkhāpada
Even if a monk is authorized, if he should exhort the nuns after sunset, there is an offense of Pācittiya.

## Bhikkhunupassaya Sikkhāpada
Whichever monk, except on the proper occasion, having gone to the nuns' quarters, should exhort the nuns, there is an offense of Pācittiya. In this case, this is the proper occasion: a nun is ill; this is the proper occasion in that case.

## Āmisa Sikkhāpada
Whichever monk should speak thus: "The elder monks exhort the nuns for the sake of material gain," there is an offense of Pācittiya.

## Cīvaradāna Sikkhāpada
Whichever monk, except in exchange, should give a robe to an unrelated nun, there is an offense of Pācittiya.

## Cīvarasibbana Sikkhāpada
Whichever monk should sew or cause to be sewn a robe for an unrelated nun, there is an offense of Pācittiya.

## Saṃvidhāna Sikkhāpada
Whichever monk, having made an appointment with a nun, should travel together on a long-distance road, even as far as the next village, except on the proper occasion, there is an offense of Pācittiya. ## Bhojana Vagga

## Āvasathapiṇḍa Sikkhāpada
A monk who is not ill may eat one meal at a public rest-house. If he should eat more than that, there is an offense of Pācittiya.

## Gaṇabhojana Sikkhāpada
For eating a group meal, except on the proper occasion, there is an offense of Pācittiya. In this case, these are the proper occasions: the occasion of being ill, the occasion of giving robes, the occasion of making robes, the occasion of traveling on a journey, the occasion of boarding a boat, the great occasion, and the occasion of a meal for ascetics; these are the proper occasions in that case.

## Paramparabhojana Sikkhāpada
For eating an out-of-turn meal, except on the proper occasion, there is an offense of Pācittiya. In this case, these are the proper occasions: the occasion of being ill, the occasion of giving robes, and the occasion of making robes; these are the proper occasions in that case.

## Kāṇamātu Sikkhāpada
If a monk, having approached a family, is invited to accept cakes or meal-powder, the monk who desires them may accept two or three bowlfuls. If he should accept more than that, there is an offense of Pācittiya. Having accepted two or three bowlfuls and having taken them from there, they must be shared with other monks; this is the proper procedure in that case.

## First Pavāraṇā Training Rule
If any monk, having eaten and being satisfied (having refused further food), should chew or consume staple or non-staple food that is not leftover (anatiritta), it is an offense of confession (pācittiya).

## Second Pavāraṇā Training Rule
If any monk, knowing that another monk has eaten and is satisfied, should invite him to eat staple or non-staple food that is not leftover, with the intention of finding fault, saying: "Here, monk, chew or eat," if the other monk eats, it is an offense of confession (pācittiya).

## Wrong-time Eating Training Rule
If any monk should chew or consume staple or non-staple food at the wrong time (after noon), it is an offense of confession (pācittiya).

## Storing Food Training Rule
If any monk should chew or consume staple or non-staple food that has been stored, it is an offense of confession (pācittiya).

## Sumptuous Food Training Rule
There are these sumptuous foods, namely: ghee, fresh butter, oil, honey, molasses, fish, meat, milk, and curd. If any monk, who is not ill, should ask for such sumptuous foods for his own sake and eat them, it is an offense of confession (pācittiya).
30:
## Tooth-stick Training Rule
If any monk should take into his mouth food that has not been offered, except for water and a tooth-stick, it is an offense of confession (pācittiya).

## The Fourth Chapter: Food.

## Naked Ascetic Chapter

## Naked Ascetic Training Rule
If any monk should give staple or non-staple food with his own hand to a naked ascetic, a male wanderer, or a female wanderer, it is an offense of confession (pācittiya).

## Dismissal Training Rule
If any monk should say to another monk, "Come, friend, let us enter the village or town for alms," and then, whether having caused food to be given to him or not, should dismiss him, saying: "Go, friend, sitting or talking with you is not pleasant for me; sitting or talking alone is more pleasant for me," if he does this solely for this reason and no other, it is an offense of confession (pācittiya).

## With-Food Training Rule
If any monk should intrude and sit in a house where a couple is present (during a meal), it is an offense of confession (pācittiya).
31:
## Secluded and Concealed Training Rule
If any monk should sit together with a woman in a secluded and concealed place, it is an offense of confession (pācittiya).

## Secluded Sitting Training Rule
If any monk should sit one-on-one with a woman in a secluded place, it is an offense of confession (pācittiya).

## Visiting Training Rule
If any monk, being invited and having a meal (to attend), should visit families before or after the meal without informing another monk who is present, except at the proper time, it is an offense of confession (pācittiya). Here, the proper time is: the time of giving robes, the time of making robes; this is the proper time in this case.

## Mahānāma Training Rule
A monk who is not ill may accept a four-month invitation for medicinal requisites, unless the invitation is renewed or is a permanent invitation. If he should accept beyond that, it is an offense of confession (pācittiya).

## Marching Army Training Rule
If any monk should go to see a marching army, except for a sufficient reason, it is an offense of confession (pācittiya).
32:
## Staying with the Army Training Rule
If there is some reason for that monk to go to the army, he may stay with the army for two or three nights. If he should stay longer than that, it is an offense of confession (pācittiya).

## Battleground Training Rule
If a monk, while staying with the army for two or three nights, should go to a battleground, a roll-call, an army array, or to see a review of the troops, it is an offense of confession (pācittiya).

## The Fifth Chapter: Naked Ascetic is finished.

## Alcohol Drinking Chapter

## Alcohol Drinking Training Rule
In the drinking of fermented or distilled liquor, there is an offense of confession (pācittiya).

## Finger-poking Training Rule
In poking with the fingers (tickling), there is an offense of confession (pācittiya).

## Water-play Training Rule
In playing in the water, there is an offense of confession (pācittiya).

## Disrespect Training Rule
In disrespect, there is an offense of confession (pācittiya).
33:
## Frightening Training Rule
If any monk should frighten a monk, it is an offense of confession (pācittiya).

## Fire Training Rule
If any monk, who is not ill, desiring to warm himself, should kindle a fire or have one kindled, except for a sufficient reason (such as lighting a lamp or firing a bowl), it is an offense of confession (pācittiya).

## Bathing Training Rule
If any monk should bathe at intervals of less than half a month, except at the proper time, it is an offense of confession (pācittiya). Here, the proper time is: the last month and a half of the hot season and the first month of the rainy season—these two and a half months are the time of heat, the time of fever; also the time of illness, the time of work, the time of traveling on a journey, the time of wind and rain; this is the proper time in this case.

## Discoloring Training Rule
When a monk receives a new robe, he must apply one of the three discoloring marks: green, mud-color, or dark brown. If a monk should use a new robe without applying one of the three discoloring marks, it is an offense of confession (pācittiya).
34:
## Vikappana Sikkhāpada

Whichever monk, having himself formally assigned a robe to a monk, or a nun, or a female trainee, or a male novice, or a female novice, should use that robe without it being rescinded (paccuddhāra), it is an offense of Pācittiya.

## Apanidhāna Sikkhāpada

Whichever monk should hide or cause to be hidden another monk's bowl, or robe, or sitting cloth, or needle case, or belt, even if only in jest, it is an offense of Pācittiya.

## The Sixth Chapter on the Drinking of Surā (Surāpāna Vagga).

## The Chapter on Living Beings (Sappāṇaka Vagga)

## Sañcicca Sikkhāpada

Whichever monk, knowing it to be a living being, should intentionally deprive an animal of life, it is an offense of Pācittiya.

## Sappāṇaka Sikkhāpada

Whichever monk, knowing that water contains living beings, should use that water, it is an offense of Pācittiya.

## Ukkoṭana Sikkhāpada

Whichever monk, knowing that a legal issue has been settled according to the Dhamma, should reopen it for further action, it is an offense of Pācittiya.

## Duṭṭhulla Sikkhāpada
35:
Whichever monk, knowing another monk's grave offense (duṭṭhulla āpatti), should conceal it, it is an offense of Pācittiya.

## Ūnavīsativassa Sikkhāpada
Whichever monk, knowing a person to be under twenty years of age, should act as preceptor and ordain him, that person is not ordained, and those monks are blameworthy; this is an offense of Pācittiya in that [act of ordaining].

## Theyyasattha Sikkhāpada
Whichever monk, knowing [them to be such], should travel by appointment with a caravan of thieves, even for the interval between one village and another, it is an offense of Pācittiya.

## Saṃvidhāna Sikkhāpada
Whichever monk should travel by appointment with a woman, even for the interval between one village and another, it is an offense of Pācittiya.

## Ariṭṭha Sikkhāpada
Whichever monk should say: "As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, those things called obstacles by the Blessed One are not able to be obstacles for one who indulges in those sexual practices," that monk should be spoken to by the monks thus: "Venerable sir, do not say such a thing; do not misrepresent the Blessed One, for misrepresentation of the Blessed One is not good; the Blessed One would not say such a thing. Friend, in many ways the Blessed One has stated that obstructive things are indeed obstacles..." to this effect he should be spoken to.
36:
"The Blessed One has stated that obstructive things are indeed obstacles, and they are certainly able to be obstacles for one who indulges in them." If that monk, when being spoken to by the monks, should persist as before, that monk should be formally admonished by the monks up to three times for the relinquishing of that view. If, being formally admonished up to three times, he relinquishes it, that is good. If he does not relinquish it, it is an offense of Pācittiya.

## Ukkhittasambhoga Sikkhāpada
Whichever monk, knowing [him to be such], should associate with, or eat with, or live with, or sleep with a monk who speaks in such a way, who has not acted according to the rule, and who has not relinquished that view (and who has been suspended), it is an offense of Pācittiya.

## Kaṇṭaka Sikkhāpada
If a novice should also say: "As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, those things called obstacles by the Blessed One are not able to be obstacles for one who indulges in them," that novice should be spoken to by the monks thus: "Friend novice, do not say such a thing; do not misrepresent the Blessed One, for misrepresentation of the Blessed One is not good; the Blessed One would not say such a thing. Friend novice, in many ways the Blessed One has stated that obstructive things are indeed obstacles, and they are certainly able to be obstacles for one who indulges in them." If that novice, when being spoken to by the monks, should persist as before, that novice should be spoken to by the monks thus: "Friend novice, from this day forth, you..."
37:
"Friend novice, from this day forth, you are not to claim the Blessed One as your teacher, nor do you have the right to sleep for two or three nights with the monks as other novices do. Go away, you lost man, be gone!" Whichever monk, knowing a novice to have been thus expelled, should entice him, or attend to him, or eat with him, or sleep with him, it is an offense of Pācittiya.

## The Seventh Chapter on Living Beings (Sappāṇaka Vagga) is finished.

## The Chapter on Fellow Monks (Sahadhammika Vagga)

## Sahadhammika Sikkhāpada
Whichever monk, when being spoken to by monks concerning a training rule that is shared by fellow monks, should say: "Friends, I will not train in this training rule until I have consulted another monk who is competent and learned in the Vinaya," it is an offense of Pācittiya. Monks, by a monk who is training, it should be understood, it should be asked, it should be investigated; this is the proper course in that training.

## Vilekhana Sikkhāpada
Whichever monk, while the Pātimokkha is being recited, should say: "What is the use of these minor and lesser training rules being recited? They only lead to remorse, distress, and confusion," it is an offense of Pācittiya for disparaging the training rules.
38:
## Mohana-sikkhāpada
If a monk, while the Pātimokkha is being recited every half-month, should say: "Only now do I know that this rule is also included in the Pāli of the Pātimokkha, is contained in the Pāli of the Pātimokkha, and comes up for recitation every half-month," he should be dealt with as follows:

If other monks know that this monk has sat through the recitation of the Pātimokkha two or three times before, not to mention more, there is no release for that monk on account of his feigned ignorance. Whatever offense he has committed therein, he should be dealt with according to the Dhamma-Vinaya. Furthermore, the charge of delusion (moha) should be imposed upon him, saying: "Friend, it is no gain for you, it is poorly gained by you, that you do not pay proper attention and take it to heart when the Pātimokkha is being recited." For that monk who feigns ignorance, this is an offense of Pācittiya.

## Pahāra-sikkhāpada
If a monk, being angry and displeased, should strike another monk, it is an offense of Pācittiya.

## Talasattika-sikkhāpada
If a monk, being angry and displeased, should raise his palm (as if to strike) against another monk, it is an offense of Pācittiya.

## Amūlaka-sikkhāpada
If a monk should accuse another monk of a Saṅghādisesa offense without grounds, it is an offense of Pācittiya.
39:
## Sañcicca-sikkhāpada
If a monk should intentionally cause remorse to another monk, thinking, "In this way, he will be uneasy even for a moment," doing it for this reason alone and no other, it is an offense of Pācittiya.

## Upassuti-sikkhāpada
If a monk should eavesdrop on monks who are engaged in a quarrel, a dispute, or a contention, thinking, "I will listen to what they say," doing it for this reason alone and no other, it is an offense of Pācittiya.

## Kammap paṭibāhana-sikkhāpada
If a monk, having given his consent to legal acts carried out in accordance with the Dhamma, should later engage in criticism, it is an offense of Pācittiya.

## Chandaṃ adatvā gamana-sikkhāpada
If a monk, while a discussion for a decision is going on in the Saṅgha, should rise from his seat and depart without having given his consent, it is an offense of Pācittiya.

## Dubbala-sikkhāpada
If a monk, having given a robe together with a harmonious Saṅgha, should later engage in criticism, saying, "The monks divert communal gains to their favorites," it is an offense of Pācittiya.
40:
## Pariṇāmana-sikkhāpada
If a monk, knowing that communal gain has been allocated to the Saṅgha, should divert it to an individual, it is an offense of Pācittiya.

## The Eighth Chapter, the Sahadhammika-vagga, is finished.

## Ratana-vagga

## Antepura-sikkhāpada
If a monk should cross the threshold of an anointed Khattiya king, from which the king has not departed and the queen has not departed, without being previously announced, it is an offense of Pācittiya.

## Ratana-sikkhāpada
If a monk should pick up or cause to be picked up a jewel or what is considered a jewel, except in a monastery or in a dwelling, it is an offense of Pācittiya. 

But if a monk has picked up or caused to be picked up a jewel or what is considered a jewel in a monastery or in a dwelling, it should be kept, thinking, "Whoever it belongs to will take it away." This is the proper procedure in that case.

## Vikālagāmappavesana-sikkhāpada
If a monk, without having asked permission from a monk who is present, should enter a village at an improper time, except on account of a suitable urgent matter, it is an offense of Pācittiya.
41:
## Sūcighara-sikkhāpada
If a monk should have a needle case made of bone, or ivory, or horn, it is an offense of Pācittiya involving breaking.

## Mañcapīṭha-sikkhāpada
When a monk is having a new bed or chair made, it should have legs eight finger-breadths high according to the Sugata's finger-breadth, excluding the lower frame. For one who exceeds that measure, it is an offense of Pācittiya involving cutting down.

## Tūlonaddha-sikkhāpada
If a monk should have a bed or chair stuffed with cotton, it is an offense of Pācittiya involving tearing out.

## Nisīdana-sikkhāpada
When a monk is having a sitting cloth made, it should be made to the proper measure. Herein, this is the measure: in length, two spans according to the Sugata's span; in width, one and a half spans; the border, one span. For one who exceeds that measure, it is an offense of Pācittiya involving cutting down.

## Kaṇḍuppaṭicchādi-sikkhāpada
When a monk is having an itch-cloth made, it should be made to the proper measure. Herein, this is the measure: in length, four spans according to the Sugata's span; in width...
42:
...two spans (it should be). For one who exceeds that measure, it is an offense of Pācittiya involving cutting down.

## Vassikasāṭika-sikkhāpada
When a monk is having a rain-cloth made, it should be made to the proper measure. Herein, this is the measure: in length, six spans according to the Sugata's span; in width, two and a half spans. For one who exceeds that measure, it is an offense of Pācittiya involving cutting down.

## Nanda-sikkhāpada
If a monk should have a robe made to the measure of the Sugata's robe, or larger, it is an offense of Pācittiya involving cutting down. Herein, this is the measure of the Sugata's robe: in length, nine spans according to the Sugata's span; in width, six spans. This is the measure of the Sugata's robe.

## Chapter on Pāṭidesanīya
## Venerable sirs, these four Pāṭidesanīya rules
## come into the recitation.
## First Pāṭidesanīya Training Rule
Should any bhikkhu, with his own hand, accept food, whether hard or soft, from the hand of an unrelated bhikkhunī who has entered within an inhabited area, and should he eat or consume it, that bhikkhu must confess: "Friend, I have committed a blameworthy, unsuitable offense that ought to be confessed; I confess it."

## Second Pāṭidesanīya Training Rule
Should bhikkhus, being invited, be eating in houses, and if that bhikkhunī stands there as if giving orders, saying: "Give curry here, give rice here," then those bhikkhus should dismiss that bhikkhunī, saying: "Sister, wait until the bhikkhus have finished eating." If not even a single bhikkhu should speak to dismiss that bhikkhunī, saying: "Sister, wait until the bhikkhus have finished eating," then those bhikkhus must confess: "Friends, we have committed a blameworthy, unsuitable offense that ought to be confessed; we confess it."

## Third Pāṭidesanīya Training Rule
There are those families designated as Sekha (learners). Should any bhikkhu, in such families designated as Sekha...
44:
...in families designated as Sekha, without being previously invited and not being ill, accept food, whether hard or soft, with his own hand, and should he eat or consume it, that bhikkhu must confess: "Friend, I have committed a blameworthy, unsuitable offense that ought to be confessed; I confess it."

## Fourth Pāṭidesanīya Training Rule
There are those forest dwellings that are considered risky and dangerous. Should any bhikkhu, in such dwellings, with his own hand, accept food, whether hard or soft, that has not been previously announced, within the monastery grounds, and should he, not being ill, eat or consume it, that bhikkhu must confess: "Friend, I have committed a blameworthy, unsuitable offense that ought to be confessed; I confess it."

Venerable sirs, the four Pāṭidesanīya rules have been recited. In respect of them, I ask the venerable sirs: Are you pure in this? A second time I ask: Are you pure in this? A third time I ask: Are you pure in this? The venerable sirs are pure in this; therefore they are silent. Thus do I record it.

## The Chapter on Pāṭidesanīya is finished.

## Settlement of Legal Processes
## Venerable sirs, these seven rules for the settlement of legal processes
## come for recitation.

For the settling and stilled ending of legal processes (adhikaraṇa) as they arise:
Removal in the presence (sammukhāvinaya) should be given.
Removal through mindfulness (sativinaya) should be given.
Removal for one who is past insanity (amūḷhavinaya) should be given.
Acting in accordance with what is admitted (paṭiññātakaraṇa) should be carried out.
The decision of the majority (yebhuyyasikā) [should be given].
The decision against one who is more depraved (tassapāpiyasikā) [should be given].
Covering over as with grass (tiṇavatthāraka) [should be given].

Venerable sirs, the seven rules for the settlement of legal processes have been recited. In respect of them, I ask the venerable sirs: Are you pure in this? A second time I ask: Are you pure in this? ## Bhikkhunī Pātimokkha Pāḷi

## Homage to that Blessed One

## 4 Preliminary Duties (Pubbakaraṇa)
Sweeping the ground, lighting the lamp, providing water, and preparing the seats—these four are called the preliminary duties (pubbakaraṇa) of the Uposatha act.

## 5 Preliminary Obligations (Pubbakicca)
Conveying consent (chanda), conveying purity (pārisuddhi), announcing the season, counting the nuns, and the exhortation (ovāda)—these five are called the preliminary obligations (pubbakicca) of the Uposatha act.

## 4 Factors of Fitness (Pattakalla)
It being the Uposatha day, as many nuns as are fit for the act being present, the absence of common offenses (sabhāgāpatti), and the absence of excluded persons in that place—these four are called the factors of fitness (pattakalla).

Having completed the preliminary duties and preliminary obligations, with the permission of the harmonious Bhikkhunī Saṅgha who have confessed their offenses, I make the request to recite the Pātimokkha.
60:
## Recitation of the Introduction
Noble ladies, let the Saṅgha listen to me. Today is the fifteenth day Uposatha. If it is the right time for the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha perform the Uposatha and recite the Pātimokkha.

What is the preliminary obligation of the Saṅgha? Noble ladies, announce your purity. I will recite the Pātimokkha; let all of us together listen well and pay attention. If any noble lady has an offense, she should reveal it. If there is no offense, she should remain silent. By her silence, I will know that the noble ladies are pure. Just as there is a reply for one who is questioned individually, so too in an assembly of this kind, it is announced up to the third time. If a nun, when it is announced up to the third time, remembers an existing offense and does not reveal it, she is guilty of conscious lying. Noble ladies, the Blessed One has said that conscious lying is an obstructive state. Therefore, an offending nun who remembers her offense and desires purity should reveal the existing offense; for when it is revealed, it becomes easy for her.

Noble ladies, the Introduction (Nidāna) has been recited. In respect of it, I ask the noble ladies: "Are you pure in this?" A second time I ask: "Are you pure in this?" A third time I ask: "Are you pure in this?" The noble ladies are pure in this; therefore they are silent. Thus do I understand that they are pure.

## The Introduction is finished.

## Recitation of the Pārājika Rules

## In this Pārājika section, these eight Pārājika rules come into recitation.

## Methunadhamma Sikkhāpada
Whatever bhikkhunī, being of shared desire, should engage in sexual intercourse, even with a male animal, she is defeated and no longer in communion.

## Adinnādāna Sikkhāpada
Whatever bhikkhunī should take from a village or from a forest what is not given, in the manner of theft—such that for taking what is not given, kings would seize the thief and kill, or bind, or banish him, saying, "You are a thief, you are a fool, you are deluded, you are a thief"—a bhikkhunī taking what is not given in such a manner is also defeated and no longer in communion.

## Manussaviggaha Sikkhāpada
Whatever bhikkhunī should intentionally deprive a human being of life, or search for a weapon for him, or praise the beauty of death, or incite him to death, saying, "My good man, what is the use of this miserable, evil life to you? Death is better for you than life," and with such a mind and such an intent, should in various ways praise the beauty of death or incite him to death, this bhikkhunī is also defeated and no longer in communion.
62:
## Training Rule on Superhuman States
Whatever bhikkhunī, without direct knowledge, should claim a superhuman state, a knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones, as being present in herself, saying, "Thus I know, thus I see"; and later, whether she is questioned or not, having fallen into an offense and desiring purification, she should say, "Sisters, not knowing, I said 'I know'; not seeing, I said 'I see'; I spoke empty lies," unless it was through overestimation, she also is defeated and no longer in communion.

## Training Rule on the Area Above the Knees
Whatever bhikkhunī, being filled with desire, should consent to a man who is also filled with desire, touching, or rubbing, or grasping, or stroking, or squeezing her below the collarbone and above the knees, she also is defeated and no longer in communion, (this is the rule) concerning the area above the knees.

## Training Rule on Concealing a Fault
Whatever bhikkhunī, knowing another bhikkhunī to have fallen into a Pārājika offense, should neither reprove her herself nor inform the group; and later, while that bhikkhunī is still remaining, or has passed away, or has been expelled, or has gone over to another sect, she should say, "Sisters, I knew before that this sister was of such and such a nature, but I did not reprove her myself, nor..."
63:
"...did I inform the group," she also is defeated and no longer in communion, (this is the rule) concerning the concealment of a fault.

## Training Rule on Following One Who is Expelled

Whatever bhikkhunī should follow a bhikkhu who has been expelled by a harmonious Saṅgha in accordance with the Dhamma, the Vinaya, and the Teacher's instruction, who is disrespectful, who has not made amends, and who is without companions; that bhikkhunī should be spoken to by the bhikkhunīs thus: "Sister, this bhikkhu has been expelled by a harmonious Saṅgha in accordance with the Dhamma, the Vinaya, and the Teacher's instruction; he is disrespectful, has not made amends, and is without companions. Sister, do not follow this bhikkhu." And if that bhikkhunī, being spoken to by the bhikkhunīs thus, should persist as before, that bhikkhunī should be admonished by the bhikkhunīs up to three times for the sake of relinquishing that course. If, being admonished up to three times, she should relinquish it, that is good. If she should not relinquish it, she also is defeated and no longer in communion, (this is the rule) concerning following one who is expelled.

## Training Rule on the Eight Grounds

Whatever bhikkhunī, being filled with desire, should consent to a man who is also filled with desire, taking her hand, or should consent to his taking the corner of her robe, or should stand with him, or should talk with him, or should go to a rendezvous, or should consent to the man's approaching her, or should enter a secluded place with him, or should dispose her body...
65:
## Corīvuṭṭhāpikāsikkhāpadaṃ
Whichever bhikkhunī, knowing a woman to be a thief sentenced to death, should ordain her (as a bhikkhunī) without having informed the king, or the Saṅgha, or a group, or an association, or a guild, except for a suitable person, this bhikkhunī also has committed an offense that is a Saṅghādisesa, which entails expulsion from the Saṅgha and is effective immediately upon commission.

## Ekagāmantaragamanasikkhāpadaṃ
Whichever bhikkhunī should go alone to another village, or should go alone to the other side of a river, or should stay away for a night alone, or should stay behind from a group alone, this bhikkhunī also has committed an offense that is a Saṅghādisesa, which entails expulsion from the Saṅgha and is effective immediately upon commission.

## Ukkhittakaosāraṇasikkhāpadaṃ
Whichever bhikkhunī, without having informed the performing Saṅgha and without knowing the consent of the group, should reinstate a bhikkhunī who has been suspended by a harmonious Saṅgha in accordance with the Dhamma, the Vinaya, and the Teacher's instruction, this bhikkhunī also has committed an offense that is a Saṅghādisesa, which entails expulsion from the Saṅgha and is effective immediately upon commission.

## Bhojanapaṭiggahaṇapaṭhamasikkhāpadaṃ
Whichever bhikkhunī, being filled with lust, should receive with her own hand food or snacks from the hand of a man who is filled with lust, and should chew or eat it, this bhikkhunī also has committed an offense that is a Saṅghādisesa, which entails expulsion from the Saṅgha and is effective immediately upon commission.
66:
## Bhojanapaṭiggahaṇadutiyasikkhāpadaṃ
Whichever bhikkhunī should speak thus: "Lady, what can this man do to you, whether he is filled with lust or not, since you are not filled with lust? Come, lady, whatever food or snacks this man gives you, receive them with your own hand and chew or eat them," (if she encourages thus), this bhikkhunī also has committed an offense that is a Saṅghādisesa, which entails expulsion from the Saṅgha and is effective immediately upon commission.

## Sañcarittasikkhāpadaṃ
Whichever bhikkhunī should practice matchmaking (sañcaritta), conveying the desires of a woman to a man, or the desires of a man to a woman, whether for marriage or for concubinage, or even for a temporary union, this bhikkhunī also has committed an offense that is a Saṅghādisesa, which entails expulsion from the Saṅgha and is effective immediately upon commission.

## Duṭṭhadosasikkhāpadaṃ
Whichever bhikkhunī, being angry and displeased with another bhikkhunī, should maliciously accuse her of a Pārājika offense without grounds, intending, "Perhaps I may cause her to fall from this holy life," and if later, whether she is cross-examined or not, that case is found to be groundless, and the bhikkhunī admits her anger, this bhikkhunī also has committed an offense that is a Saṅghādisesa, which entails expulsion from the Saṅgha and is effective immediately upon commission.

## Aññabhāgiyasikkhāpadaṃ
Whichever bhikkhunī, being angry and displeased with another bhikkhunī, taking some minor point of a different case...
67:
...and using it as a pretext to accuse her of a Pārājika offense, intending, "Perhaps I may cause her to fall from this holy life," and if later, whether she is cross-examined or not, that case is found to be of a different nature (groundless), and even if a minor point was taken, and the bhikkhunī persists in her anger, this bhikkhunī also has committed an offense that is a Saṅghādisesa, which entails expulsion from the Saṅgha and is effective immediately upon commission.

## Training Rule on Renouncing the Training
Whichever bhikkhunī, being angry and displeased, should speak thus: "I renounce the Buddha, I renounce the Dhamma, I renounce the Saṅgha, I renounce the training. Are only these Sakyan daughters bhikkhunīs? There are other bhikkhunīs who are modest, scrupulous, and desirous of training; I will live the holy life in their presence." That bhikkhunī should be spoken to by the bhikkhunīs thus: "Lady, do not be angry and displeased and speak thus: 'I renounce the Buddha... I will live the holy life in their presence.' Lady, delight (in the training); the Dhamma is well-expounded; live the holy life for the sake of making an end of suffering." If that bhikkhunī, being spoken to by the bhikkhunīs, should still persist as before, that bhikkhunī should be admonished by the bhikkhunīs up to three times for the sake of giving up that course.
68:
If, being admonished up to three times, she should give up that course, that is good. If she should not give it up, this bhikkhunī also has committed an offense that is a Saṅghādisesa, which entails expulsion from the Saṅgha and is effective after the third admonition.

## Training Rule on Anger due to a Legal Issue
Whichever bhikkhunī, having lost a certain legal case, being angry and displeased, should speak thus: "The bhikkhunīs follow favoritism, the bhikkhunīs follow malice, the bhikkhunīs follow delusion, the bhikkhunīs follow fear." That bhikkhunī should be spoken to by the bhikkhunīs thus: "Lady, do not be angry and displeased because you lost a certain legal case and speak thus: 'The bhikkhunīs follow favoritism... fear.' Lady, you yourself might follow favoritism, you might follow malice, you might follow delusion, you might follow fear." If that bhikkhunī, being spoken to by the bhikkhunīs, should still persist as before, that bhikkhunī should be admonished by the bhikkhunīs up to three times for the sake of giving up that course. If, being admonished up to three times, she should give up that course, that is good. If she should not give it up, this bhikkhunī also has committed an offense that is a Saṅghādisesa, which entails expulsion from the Saṅgha and is effective after the third admonition.
69:
## First Training Rule on Evil Conduct

If bhikkhunīs live in association [with laypeople], having evil conduct, evil reputation, and evil livelihood, harassing the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha, and concealing each other's faults, those bhikkhunīs should be told by the bhikkhunīs: "Sisters, you are living in association, having evil conduct, evil reputation, and evil livelihood, harassing the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha, and concealing each other's faults. Sisters, live apart; the Saṅgha praises only seclusion for the sisters."

If those bhikkhunīs, when being spoken to by the bhikkhunīs, still persist as before, those bhikkhunīs should be formally admonished up to three times by the bhikkhunīs for the purpose of relinquishing that [conduct]. If, while being formally admonished up to three times, they relinquish it, that is good. If they do not relinquish it, these bhikkhunīs also incur an offense of Saṅghādisesa involving expulsion, which is reached at the third formal admonition.

## Second Training Rule on Evil Conduct

If a bhikkhunī should say: "Sisters, do live in association; do not live apart. There are other bhikkhunīs in the Saṅgha who have such conduct, such reputation, such livelihood, who harass the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha and conceal each other's faults. The Saṅgha says nothing to them, but the Saṅgha says this to you only because of contempt, hatred, intolerance, because of [the Saṅgha] being powerful, and because of [you] being weak: 'Sisters, you are living in association, having evil conduct, evil reputation, and evil livelihood..."
70:
...harassing the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha, and concealing each other's faults. Sisters, live apart; the Saṅgha praises only seclusion for the sisters.'"

That bhikkhunī should be told by the bhikkhunīs: "Sister, do not say so. Do not say: 'Sisters, do live in association; do not live apart. There are other bhikkhunīs in the Saṅgha who have such conduct, such reputation, such livelihood, who harass the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha and conceal each other's faults. The Saṅgha says nothing to them, but the Saṅgha says this to you only because of contempt, hatred, intolerance, because of [the Saṅgha] being powerful, and because of [you] being weak: "Sisters, you are living in association, having evil conduct, evil reputation, and evil livelihood, harassing the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha, and concealing each other's faults. Sisters, live apart; the Saṅgha praises only seclusion for the sisters."'"

If that bhikkhunī, when being spoken to by the bhikkhunīs, still persists as before, that bhikkhunī should be formally admonished up to three times by the bhikkhunīs for the purpose of relinquishing that [conduct]. If, while being formally admonished up to three times, she relinquishes it, that is good. If she does not relinquish it, this bhikkhunī also incurs an offense of Saṅghādisesa involving expulsion, which is reached at the third formal admonition.

## Training Rule on Schism in the Saṅgha

If a bhikkhunī should strive for a schism of a harmonious Saṅgha, or should persist in taking up and supporting a cause or a legal issue (adhikaraṇa) conducive to a schism, that bhikkhunī should be told by the bhikkhunīs: "Sister, do not strive for a schism of a harmonious Saṅgha..."
71:
...or persist in taking up and supporting a legal issue conducive to a schism. "Sister, be reconciled with the Saṅgha. For a harmonious Saṅgha, being in agreement and without dispute, lives happily under a single recitation (uddesa)."

If that bhikkhunī, when being spoken to by the bhikkhunīs, still persists as before, that bhikkhunī should be formally admonished up to three times by the bhikkhunīs for the purpose of relinquishing that [view]. If, while being formally admonished up to three times, she relinquishes it, that is good. If she does not relinquish it, this bhikkhunī also incurs an offense of Saṅghādisesa involving expulsion, which is reached at the third formal admonition.

## Training Rule on Following a Schismatic

If there are bhikkhunīs—one, two, or three—who are followers of that [schismatic] bhikkhunī and who speak on the side of the faction, and they should say: "Sisters, do not say anything to this bhikkhunī. This bhikkhunī is a speaker of Dhamma; this bhikkhunī is a speaker of Vinaya. This bhikkhunī speaks after taking our desire and preference; she knows and speaks, she does not speak without knowing; and this [speech] is pleasing to us."

Those bhikkhunīs should be told by the bhikkhunīs: "Sisters, do not say so. This bhikkhunī is not a speaker of Dhamma; this bhikkhunī is not a speaker of Vinaya. Sisters, let not a schism in the Saṅgha be pleasing to you. Sisters, be reconciled with the Saṅgha. For a harmonious Saṅgha, being in agreement and without dispute, lives happily under a single recitation."

If those bhikkhunīs, when being spoken to by the bhikkhunīs, still persist as before, those bhikkhunīs should be [formally admonished] up to three times...
72:
...they should be formally admonished up to three times for the relinquishing of that view. If, while being formally admonished up to three times, they relinquish that view, that is good. If they do not relinquish it, these bhikkhunīs also have committed an offense of Saṅghādisesa entailing expulsion, which is completed upon the third admonishment.

## Dubbaca Sikkhāpada

Furthermore, if a bhikkhunī is of a nature difficult to speak to, and when being spoken to by bhikkhunīs according to the Dhamma regarding the training rules included in the Pātimokkha, she makes herself unadmonishable, saying: "Ladies, do not say anything to me, whether good or bad; and I, ladies, will not say anything to you, whether good or bad. Refrain, ladies, from speaking to me." That bhikkhunī should be spoken to by the bhikkhunīs thus: "Lady, do not make yourself unadmonishable. Lady, make yourself admonishable. May the lady also speak to the bhikkhunīs according to the Dhamma, and the bhikkhunīs will also speak to the lady according to the Dhamma. For it is by such mutual speech and mutual rehabilitation from offenses that the assembly of the Blessed One has grown, that is to say, by mutual admonition and mutual rising from offenses." If that bhikkhunī, when being spoken to by the bhikkhunīs in this way, persists as before (making herself unadmonishable), she should be formally admonished by the bhikkhunīs up to three times for the relinquishing of that view. If, while being formally admonished up to three times, she relinquishes that view, that is good. If she does not relinquish it, this bhikkhunī also has committed an offense of Saṅghādisesa entailing expulsion, which is completed upon the third admonishment.
73:
## Kuladūsaka Sikkhāpada

A bhikkhunī lives depending on a certain village or town, being a corrupter of families and of evil conduct. Her evil conduct is both seen and heard, and the families corrupted by her are both seen and heard. That bhikkhunī should be spoken to by the bhikkhunīs thus: "Lady, you are a corrupter of families and of evil conduct. Your evil conduct is both seen and heard, and the families corrupted by you are both seen and heard. Depart, lady, from this monastery; your staying here is of no use."

If, when being spoken to by the bhikkhunīs in this way, that bhikkhunī should say to those bhikkhunīs: "The bhikkhunīs follow favoritism, the bhikkhunīs follow malice, the bhikkhunīs follow delusion, the bhikkhunīs follow fear. For such an offense, they expel some and do not expel others."

That bhikkhunī should be spoken to by the bhikkhunīs thus: "Lady, do not say so. The bhikkhunīs do not follow favoritism, the bhikkhunīs do not follow malice, the bhikkhunīs do not follow delusion, the bhikkhunīs do not follow fear. You, lady, are a corrupter of families and of evil conduct. Your evil conduct is both seen and heard, and the families corrupted by you are both seen and heard. Depart, lady, from this monastery; your staying here is of no use."

If, when being spoken to by the bhikkhunīs in this way, that bhikkhunī persists as before, she should be formally admonished by the bhikkhunīs up to three times for the relinquishing of that view. If, while being formally admonished up to three times...
74:
...while being formally admonished, if she relinquishes that view, that is good. If she does not relinquish it, this bhikkhunī also has committed an offense of Saṅghādisesa entailing expulsion, which is completed upon the third admonishment.

## Ladies, the seventeen Saṅghādisesa rules have been recited. Nine are offenses upon the first commission, and eight become offenses after the third formal admonishment.

If a bhikkhunī falls into any one of these offenses, she must undergo the fortnightly penance (mānatta) before both Saṅghas. When the bhikkhunī has undergone the penance, she must be rehabilitated (abbhāna) in a place where there is a community of twenty bhikkhunīs. If a community of bhikkhunīs numbering even one less than twenty should rehabilitate that bhikkhunī, she is not rehabilitated, and those bhikkhunīs are blameworthy. This is the proper procedure there.

In this matter, I ask the ladies: "Are you pure in this?" A second time I ask: "Are you pure in this?" A third time I ask: "Are you pure in this?" The ladies are pure in this, therefore they are silent. Thus I record it.

## The Chapter on Saṅghādisesa is finished.

## The Chapter on Nissaggiya Pācittiya

## Ladies, these thirty Nissaggiya Pācittiya rules

## come into recitation.

## Pattasannicaya Sikkhāpada

If a bhikkhunī should hoard bowls, she commits an offense of Nissaggiya Pācittiya.
75:
## Akālacīvarabhājana Sikkhāpada
If a bhikkhunī, having assigned an out-of-season robe as an 'in-season robe', has it distributed, she commits an offense of Expiation with Forfeiture (Nissaggiya Pācittiya).

## Cīvaraparivattana Sikkhāpada
If a bhikkhunī exchanges a robe with another bhikkhunī, and later says to her: "Here, lady, is your robe; give me that robe of mine; what is yours is yours, what is mine is mine; give me that robe of mine; take back your own," and if she snatches it back herself or has it snatched back, she commits an offense of Expiation with Forfeiture.

## Aññaviññāpana Sikkhāpada
If a bhikkhunī, having asked for one thing, asks for another thing (from the same donor), she commits an offense of Expiation with Forfeiture.

## Aññacetāpana Sikkhāpada
If a bhikkhunī, having had one thing bartered, has another thing bartered (from the same person), she commits an offense of Expiation with Forfeiture.

## Paṭhamasaṅghikacetāpana Sikkhāpada
If a bhikkhunī barters for something else with a requisite intended for another purpose, designated for another thing, and donated to the Saṅgha, she commits an offense of Expiation with Forfeiture.
76:
## Dutiyasaṅghikacetāpana Sikkhāpada
If a bhikkhunī barters for something else with two types of requisites intended for another purpose, donated to the Saṅgha, and requested by herself, she commits an offense of Expiation with Forfeiture.

## Paṭhamagaṇikacetāpana Sikkhāpada
If a bhikkhunī barters for something else with a requisite intended for another purpose, donated to a group (gaṇa) of bhikkhunīs, she commits an offense of Expiation with Forfeiture.

## Dutiyagaṇikacetāpana Sikkhāpada
If a bhikkhunī barters for something else with two types of requisites intended for another purpose, donated to a group (gaṇa) of bhikkhunīs, and requested by herself, she commits an offense of Expiation with Forfeiture.

## Puggalikacetāpana Sikkhāpada
If a bhikkhunī barters for something else with two types of requisites intended for another purpose, donated to an individual, and requested by herself, she commits an offense of Expiation with Forfeiture.

## Patta-vagga the First
The first chapter on bowls is finished.

## Garupāvuraṇa Sikkhāpada
A bhikkhunī who is bartering for a heavy cloak should barter for one worth at most four kaṃsas (16 kyats). If she barters for one worth more than that, she commits an offense of Expiation with Forfeiture.
77:
## Lahupāvuraṇa Sikkhāpada
A bhikkhunī who is bartering for a light cloak should barter for one worth at most two and a half kaṃsas (10 kyats). If she barters for one worth more than that, she commits an offense of Expiation with Forfeiture.

## Kathina Sikkhāpada
When a bhikkhunī's robe is finished and the kathina has been removed, an extra robe may be kept for at most ten days. For a bhikkhunī who lets that period exceed ten days, she commits an offense of Expiation with Forfeiture.

## Udositā Sikkhāpada
When a bhikkhunī's robe is finished and the kathina has been removed, if a bhikkhunī stays apart from her three robes even for one night, except with the agreement of the bhikkhunīs, she commits an offense of Expiation with Forfeiture.

## Akālacīvara Sikkhāpada
When a bhikkhunī's robe is finished and the kathina has been removed, if an out-of-season robe (akālacīvara) accrues to a bhikkhunī, it may be accepted by a bhikkhunī who desires it. Having accepted it, it should be made up quickly. If that robe is not sufficient and there is hope of completing it, it may be kept by that bhikkhunī for at most one month to complete the deficiency. If she keeps it for more than a month even if there is hope, she commits an offense of Expiation with Forfeiture.

## Aññātakaviññatti Sikkhāpada
If a bhikkhunī asks for a robe from a male householder or a female householder who is not a relative, except at the right time,
78:
she commits an offense of Expiation with Forfeiture. In this case, the right time is when the bhikkhunī's robe has been snatched away or her robe has been lost; this is the right time in this case.

## Tatuttari Sikkhāpada
If a male householder or a female householder who is not a relative invites that bhikkhunī with many robes, she should accept at most two robes from them—an inner and an upper robe (santaruttara). If she accepts more than that, she commits an offense of Expiation with Forfeiture.

## Paṭhamaupakkhaṭa Sikkhāpada
A robe-fund has been prepared by a male or female householder who is not a relative, intended for a bhikkhunī, thinking: "I will barter for a robe with this robe-fund and provide a robe for the bhikkhunī named so-and-so." If that bhikkhunī, without being invited beforehand, approaches them and makes a suggestion regarding the robe, saying: "It would be good, sir, if you barter for such and such a robe with this robe-fund and provide it for me," out of a desire for a fine robe, she commits an offense of Expiation with Forfeiture.

## Dutiyaupakkhaṭa Sikkhāpada
Two male householders or two female householders who are not relatives have individual robe-funds prepared for a bhikkhunī, thinking: "We will barter for individual robes with these individual robe-funds and (provide them) for the bhikkhunī named so-and-so."
79:
"...we shall provide you with robes." In that regard, if that bhikkhunī, without being previously invited, approaches them and makes a specific arrangement regarding the robes, saying: "Indeed, it would be good, sirs, if you would purchase such and such a robe with these separate robe-funds and provide me with one robe together," out of a desire for something fine, it is an offence of expiation involving forfeiture (Nissaggiya Pācittiya).

## Rājasikkhāpada (The Training Rule concerning Kings)

Suppose a king, a royal official, a brahmin, or a householder sends a robe-fund for a bhikkhunī by a messenger, saying: "Having purchased a robe with this robe-fund, provide the bhikkhunī named so-and-so with a robe." If that messenger approaches that bhikkhunī and says: "Lady, this robe-fund has been brought for you; lady, please accept this robe-fund." That bhikkhunī should say to that messenger: "Friend, we do not accept robe-funds; we accept robes at the proper time if they are allowable." If that messenger says to that bhikkhunī: "Lady, is there anyone who is your steward (veyyāvaccakara)?" Monks, a bhikkhunī who is in need of a robe should point out a steward, either a monastery attendant (ārāmika) or a lay follower (upāsaka), saying: "Friend, this person is the steward for the bhikkhunīs." If that messenger, having instructed the steward, approaches that bhikkhunī and says: "Lady, I have instructed the steward whom you pointed out;"
80:
"Lady, please approach him at the proper time, and he will provide you with a robe." Monks, a bhikkhunī who is in need of a robe, having approached the steward, should prompt and remind him two or three times, saying: "Friend, I have need of a robe." If, while prompting and reminding him two or three times, she obtains the robe, that is good. If she does not obtain it, she should stand in silence for the purpose [of receiving the robe] four times, five times, or at most six times. If, while standing in silence for the purpose four, five, or at most six times, she obtains the robe, that is good. If she exerts further effort beyond that and obtains the robe, it is an offence of expiation involving forfeiture (Nissaggiya Pācittiya). If she does not obtain it, she should either go herself or send a messenger to the place from where the robe-fund was brought for her, saying: "Sirs, the robe-fund that you sent for the bhikkhunī has not benefited that bhikkhunī in any way. May you reclaim your own property; do not let your property be lost." This is the proper procedure (sāmīci) in this case.

## Cīvaravagga (The Second Chapter on Robes) is finished.

## Rūpiyasikkhāpada (The Training Rule on Gold and Silver)

Whichever bhikkhunī should pick up gold or silver, or have it picked up, or should consent to it being deposited [for her], it is an offence of expiation involving forfeiture (Nissaggiya Pācittiya).
81:
## Rūpiyasaṃvohārasikkhāpada (The Training Rule on Monetary Exchange)

Whichever bhikkhunī should engage in various types of monetary exchange involving gold and silver, it is an offence of expiation involving forfeiture (Nissaggiya Pācittiya).

## Kayavikkayasikkhāpada (The Training Rule on Buying and Selling)

Whichever bhikkhunī should engage in various types of buying and selling, it is an offence of expiation involving forfeiture (Nissaggiya Pācittiya).

## Ūnapañcabandhanasikkhāpada (The Training Rule on a Bowl with Fewer than Five Mends)

Whichever bhikkhunī should ask for another new bowl when her bowl has fewer than five mends, it is an offence of expiation involving forfeiture (Nissaggiya Pācittiya). That bowl must be forfeited by that bhikkhunī to the community of bhikkhunīs. Whichever is the last (worst) bowl in that community of bhikkhunīs should be given to that bhikkhunī with the instruction: "Bhikkhunī, this bowl is to be used by you until it breaks." This is the proper procedure in this case.

## Bhesajjasikkhāpada (The Training Rule on Medicines)

There are these medicines to be used by sick bhikkhunīs, namely: ghee, butter, oil, honey, and molasses. Having accepted them, they may be stored and consumed for at most seven days. For the bhikkhunī who exceeds those seven days, it is an offence of expiation involving forfeiture (Nissaggiya Pācittiya).
82:
## Cīvara-acchindanasikkhāpada (The Training Rule on Snatching back a Robe)

Whichever bhikkhunī, having herself given a robe to another bhikkhunī, should, being angry or displeased, snatch it back or have it snatched back, it is an offence of expiation involving forfeiture (Nissaggiya Pācittiya).

## Suttaviññattisikkhāpada (The Training Rule on Requesting Thread)

Whichever bhikkhunī, having herself requested thread, should have weavers weave a robe, it is an offence of expiation involving forfeiture (Nissaggiya Pācittiya).

## Mahāpesakārasikkhāpada (The Great Rule on Weavers)

Suppose a householder or a householder's wife, who is not a relative, has weavers weave a robe specifically for a bhikkhunī. If that bhikkhunī, without being previously invited, approaches the weavers and makes a specific arrangement regarding the robe, saying: "Friends, this robe is being woven for me; make it long, make it wide, make it thick, make it well-woven, make it well-combed, make it well-scraped, and make it well-finished. Perhaps we might give you some small gift." If that bhikkhunī, having spoken thus, gives some small gift, even as little as a single alms-meal, it is an offence of expiation involving forfeiture (Nissaggiya Pācittiya).

## Accekacīvarasikkhāpada (The Training Rule on Urgent Robes)

If an urgent robe should accrue to a bhikkhunī ten days before the full moon of the month of Kattika, it may be accepted by the bhikkhunī who considers it an urgent robe. Having accepted it, it may be kept until the robe-season. If she should keep it beyond that, it is an offence of expiation involving forfeiture (Nissaggiya Pācittiya).
83:
## Pariṇata Sikkhāpada
Whichever nun, knowing that a gain has been diverted to the Saṅgha, should divert it to herself, it is an offence of confession involving forfeiture (Nissaggiya Pācittiya).

## Patta Vagga, the Third.
Ladies, the thirty rules of confession involving forfeiture have been recited. In respect of them, I ask the ladies: Are you pure in this? A second time I ask: Are you pure in this? A third time I ask: Are you pure in this? The ladies are pure in this; therefore they are silent. Thus do I understand this.

## The Nissaggiya Pācittiya section is finished.

## Suddha Pācittiyā
The section on Pure Confession.

## Now, ladies, these one hundred and sixty-six rules of confession

## come into recitation.

## Lasuṇa Vagga
The Garlic Chapter

## Lasuṇa Sikkhāpada
Whichever nun should eat garlic, it is an offence of confession (Pācittiya).

## Sambhādhaloma Sikkhāpada
Whichever nun should have the hair in the private parts removed, it is an offence of confession.

## Talaghātaka Sikkhāpada
In the case of striking with the palm (on the private parts), it is an offence of confession.
84:
## Jatumaṭṭhaka Sikkhāpada
In the case of (inserting) a smooth lac-stick (into the private parts), it is an offence of confession.

## Udakasuddhika Sikkhāpada
A nun who is cleansing herself with water should insert it only to the extent of two finger-joints. For one who exceeds that limit, it is an offence of confession.

## Upatiṭṭhana Sikkhāpada
Whichever nun should stand in attendance near a monk who is eating, with drinking water or a fan, it is an offence of confession.

## Āmakadhanya Sikkhāpada
Whichever nun, having asked for raw grain herself or having had someone else ask for it, having roasted it herself or having had someone else roast it, having pounded it herself or having had someone else pound it, having cooked it herself or having had someone else cook it, should eat it, it is an offence of confession.

## Paṭhama Uccārasaḍḍhana Sikkhāpada
Whichever nun should herself throw, or cause another to throw, excrement, urine, rubbish, or food scraps over a wall or over a fence, it is an offence of confession.

## Dutiya Uccārasaḍḍhana Sikkhāpada
Whichever nun should herself throw, or cause another to throw, excrement, urine, rubbish, or food scraps on green crops, it is an offence of confession.
85:
## Naccagīta Sikkhāpada
Whichever nun should go to see dancing, singing, or music, it is an offence of confession for that nun.

## Lasuṇa Vaggo Paṭhamo.
The First Chapter, on Garlic (is finished).

## Rattandhakāra Vagga
The Chapter on the Darkness of Night.

## Rattandhakāra Sikkhāpada
Whichever nun should stand or talk alone with a man in the darkness of night in a place where there is no light such as a lamp, it is an offence of confession for that nun.

## Paṭicchannokāsa Sikkhāpada
Whichever nun should stand or talk alone with a man in a concealed place, it is an offence of confession for that nun.

## Ajjhokāsasallapana Sikkhāpada
Whichever nun should stand or talk alone with a man in the open air, it is an offence of confession for that nun.

## Dutiyikauyyojana Sikkhāpada
Whichever nun should stand or talk alone with a man in a carriage road, a cul-de-sac, or at a crossroads, or should whisper in his ear, or should send away the nun who is her companion, it is an offence of confession for that nun.
86:
## Anāpucchāpakkamana Sikkhāpada
Whichever nun, having approached families in the morning before noon and having sat down on a seat, should depart without informing the owners, it is an offence of confession.

## Anāpucchāabhinisīdana Sikkhāpada
Whichever nun, having approached families in the afternoon and having sat down or lain down on a seat without informing the owners, it is an offence of confession.

## Anāpucchāsantharaṇa Sikkhāpada
Whichever nun, having approached families at an unseasonable time after sunset and having spread out bedding herself or having had it spread out, should sit down or lie down without informing the owners, it is an offence of confession.

## Paraujjhāpanaka Sikkhāpada
Whichever nun, through wrong perception or wrong understanding, should cause another nun to be criticized, it is an offence of confession.

## Paraabhisapana Sikkhāpada
Whichever nun should curse herself or another with hell or with the holy life (Brahmacariya), it is an offence of confession.

## Rodana Sikkhāpada
Whichever nun should cry while repeatedly striking herself, it is an offence of confession.

## Rattandhakāra Vaggo Dutiyo.
The Second Chapter, on the Darkness of Night, is finished.
87:
## Nagga Vagga
The Nakedness Chapter

## Nagga Sikkhāpada
Whichever nun should bathe naked, it is an offence of confession.

## Udakasāṭika Sikkhāpada
A nun who is having a water-cloth made should have it made to the proper measurement. Herein, this is the measurement: four spans in length according to the Sugata's span, and two spans in width. For one who exceeds that measurement, it is an offence of confession involving cutting down (Chendanaka Pācittiya).

## Cīvarasibbana Sikkhāpada
Whichever nun, having unpicked a nun's robe herself or having had it unpicked, and later, when there is no obstacle, should neither sew it herself nor make an effort to have it sewn for four or five days, it is an offence of confession.

## Saṅghāṭicāra Sikkhāpada
Whichever nun should exceed five days without wearing or rotating her outer robes (Saṅghāṭi), it is an offence of confession.

## Cīvarasaṅkamanīya Sikkhāpada
Whichever nun should wear a robe that should be transferred (returned), it is an offence of confession.

## Gaṇacīvara Sikkhāpada
Whichever nun should cause an obstacle to the gain of robes for the group (Gaṇa), it is an offence of confession.
88:
## Paṭibāhana Sikkhāpada
If a bhikkhunī should obstruct the distribution of robes in accordance with the Dhamma, she commits a pācittiya offence.

## Cīvaradāna Sikkhāpada
If a bhikkhunī should give a monastic robe to a layperson, or to a male wanderer, or to a female wanderer, she commits a pācittiya offence.

## Kāla-atikkamana Sikkhāpada
If a bhikkhunī, with a weak hope of obtaining a robe, should let the robe-time pass, she commits a pācittiya offence.

## Kaṭhinuddhāra Sikkhāpada
If a bhikkhunī should obstruct the removal of the Kaṭhina in accordance with the Dhamma, she commits a pācittiya offence.

## Ekamañcatuvaṭṭana Sikkhāpada
If two bhikkhunīs should lie down together on a single bed, they commit a pācittiya offence.

## Ekattharaṇatuvaṭṭana Sikkhāpada
If two bhikkhunīs should lie down together using a single spread and a single cover, they commit a pācittiya offence.
90:
